doc_summary: Buck Shlegeris explains why his AI control work assumes a capable, coordinated, well-informed adversary (a conservative red team), while still measuring rather than assuming the model's ability to execute attacks. He weighs the methodological cleanliness of this against its costs and says about half of control research should use it.

items.claim: Prefers measuring a model's actual ability to execute a specific attack strategy over assuming it is arbitrarily capable, because assuming worst-case capability would force 'safety is zero' and give no usable estimate.
items.quote: We don’t therefore say “safety is zero, because we’ve demonstrated that there are actions that the AI could output that would be catastrophic”. Instead, we measure the proportion of the time that the scaffold’s code gets past all the safety measures

items.claim: In a setup, give the red team broad affordances when building the attack policy but hold out the specific evaluation inputs, because the policy must adapt to actual situations rather than being tuned to the test instances.
items.quote: they’re allowed to look at the input distribution, to iterate against the trusted monitor, to use game theory to calculate optimal attack rates—but the red team is not allowed to see the particular inputs where the control evaluation will be run.

items.claim: Prefers evaluations built on easy-to-measure capability assumptions over ones that depend on hard-to-test properties, because the latter let developers make flawed or cherry-picked safety arguments from weak, illegible evidence.
items.quote: Assessing all those assumptions is much harder and more conceptually confusing than doing the capability evaluation required to analyze a single proposed attack plan.

items.claim: Distrusts capability evaluations that may teach the model new skills (overestimation) or let a scheming model hide ability (underestimation), so they require large diverse task spaces and train-eval separation.
items.quote: But we might overestimate capabilities if our evaluation process is actually teaching new skills rather than measuring existing ones. To prevent this, we need a large space of possible tasks within the capability domain we're testing

items.claim: Assumes the model knows its deployment context (organization, safety measures, input distribution) because pretraining data, targeted training, and observable interventions would likely reveal it, so tests should not rely on hiding this.
items.quote: Some safety measures are implicitly visible to them (e.g. if we use techniques that sometimes replace their actions with the actions of a different model, they’ll probably notice this).

items.claim: Prefers designing under the assumption that the adversary knows the system in detail over security through obscurity, because obscurity is not a robust basis for safety (Kerckhoffs's principle), though he notes AI information flow may be more controllable.
items.quote: design your system assuming that your opponents know it in detail.

items.claim: Spend most effort on conservative-assumption evaluations, then upweight techniques that only work if assumptions fail in an ad hoc way, because classic control evals systematically undervalue such techniques.
items.quote: the right way to handle this (when thinking about dangerously capable models) is to spend most of your time making the conservative assumptions, and then upweight these non-conservatively-evaluated techniques in an ad hoc manner.

items.claim: Distrusts evaluation methodology that grants the red team unrealistically strong tools (e.g. ad-hoc adversarial example generation), since resulting attack policies may exceed what is realistically expected.
items.quote: if we allow the red-team to use adversarial example generation techniques to find universal jailbreaks and teach those to the untrusted models, the attack policies might be much more capable than we should realistically expect.

items.claim: Thinks conservative worst-case assumptions should be only about half of control research, with the rest targeting earlier, less competent and coherent schemers where worst-case assumptions are unreasonable.
items.quote: I currently think that about half of the AI control research should make these conservative assumptions. But I’m less enthusiastic about these assumptions than I was a year ago.

items.claim: Proposes ways to get around the limited diversity of strategic capabilities in evals: broaden training sets, use analogous capabilities, draw scaling curves, and try harder with few examples.
items.quote:
Broaden your training set to less important strategic capabilities
Evaluate on analogous capabilities that we think are similarly difficult
Draw scaling curves
